Main-effects generalizability approximation for an MFRM design

Source: R/api-generalizability.R, R/api-gstudy-entry.R
mfrm_generalizability.Rd

Re-fits the rating data underlying an mfrm_fit as a crossed random-effects model Score ~ 1 + (1 | Person) + (1 | Facet1) + ... + Residual via lme4::lmer, and returns main-effect variance components, residual variance, and G / Phi coefficients under this simplified model. Interactions are not estimated separately. For a G-study including the supported interactions, use mfrm_g_study() with one or two common random facets; it also accepts a single score column.

mfrm_d_study() applies a practical D-study projection to the variance components from mfrm_generalizability(). It answers questions such as "what happens to G and Phi if we use 2, 3, or 4 raters?" without re-fitting the Rasch/MFRM model.

Compare planned facet counts using an existing mfrm_d_study() result. G concerns relative ordering; Phi also includes shifts in absolute score levels. Larger coefficients mean greater dependability under the selected model and residual assumption, not proven pass/fail accuracy.

Usage

mfrm_generalizability(
  fit,
  data = NULL,
  object_facet = "Person",
  random_facets = NULL,
  reml = TRUE,
  missing = c("error", "omit")
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_generalizability'
mfrm_d_study(
  x,
  design_grid = NULL,
  residual_scaling = c("highest_order", "single_condition", "none", "sensitivity"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_d_study'
plot(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  type = c("coefficients", "error_variance", "heatmap", "contour", "surface3d"),
  x_var = NULL,
  y_var = NULL,
  group_var = NULL,
  panel_by = NULL,
  panel_grid = NULL,
  metric = NULL,
  draw = TRUE,
  main = NULL,
  palette = NULL,
  preset = c("standard", "publication", "compact", "monochrome"),
  reference = NULL,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_fit'
mfrm_d_study(
  x,
  design_grid = NULL,
  object_facet = "Person",
  random_facets = NULL,
  residual_scaling = c("highest_order", "single_condition", "none", "sensitivity"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_d_study'
summary(object, ...)

Arguments

fit

An mfrm_fit from fit_mfrm().

data

Optional data frame. When NULL, the rating data stored on fit$prep$data is used. Required columns are the selected facets and Score. Scores must be numeric or numeric character/factor labels; nonnumeric labels and infinite values are refused. Use NA for missing values. Facet labels must be nonblank; Score and Residual are reserved and cannot be facet names.

object_facet

Passed to mfrm_generalizability() when x is an mfrm_fit.

random_facets

Passed to mfrm_generalizability() when x is an mfrm_fit.

reml

Logical, passed to lme4::lmer() (default TRUE).

missing

Either "error" (default) or "omit". Missing scores or selected facet values stop the analysis by default. Explicit omission fits only complete rows and records the excluded row positions and missing columns. Missingness in unselected columns does not exclude a row.

x

An mfrm_d_study() result.

design_grid

Data frame or named list giving planned counts for each random measurement facet. Column names may be the facet names themselves (for example Rater) or n_ plus the facet name (for example n_Rater). Supply exactly one count column per facet, with unique names and an unambiguous one-to-one correspondence. Extra columns, duplicate aliases for a facet, or a column serving two facets are refused. Counts must be positive integers. When NULL, one row using the observed number of levels is returned.

residual_scaling

How the collapsed residual variance should be scaled when planned facet counts increase. "highest_order" treats the residual as highest-order person-by-all-conditions/error variance and divides by the product of planned counts. "single_condition" divides by the smallest planned facet count, a sensitivity assumption for variation associated with the least-replicated condition. It is not a confidence bound. "none" leaves the residual unscaled. "sensitivity" returns all three assumptions for each design row.

...

Reserved for method compatibility.

y

Reserved for method compatibility.

type

"coefficients" for G/Phi curves, "error_variance" for error variance curves, or "heatmap", "contour", or "surface3d" for one metric over two facet counts. Error variance is in squared score units, not SEM. Lower error variance is better.

x_var

Planned-count columns such as "n_Rater". The default horizontal axis is the first count column; surface plots use the next column on the other axis. The two axes must differ.

y_var

Planned-count columns such as "n_Rater". The default horizontal axis is the first count column; surface plots use the next column on the other axis. The two axes must differ.

group_var

Optional additional column distinguishing curves. All non-horizontal facet counts and residual assumptions remain separate within each panel, including when group_var is supplied.

panel_by

One column defining panels, or NULL.

panel_grid

One or two columns defining panels. Use this or panel_by, not both. Surface plots require every other facet count and residual assumption to be constant within each panel. Subset the result or add panels when they vary; they cannot be silently averaged or overlaid.

metric

Optional selection from "G", "Phi", "RelativeErrorVariance", or "AbsoluteErrorVariance", compatible with type. Surface plots require one metric and default to "Phi".

draw

Draw when TRUE; FALSE only returns plot data.

main

Optional plot title.

palette

Optional colors.

preset

Plot style: "standard", "publication", "compact", or "monochrome".

reference

Optional distinct finite numeric reference values for curves, between 0 and 1 for coefficients or nonnegative for error variance. NULL draws no guides. Not supported for surface plots.

object

A main-effects D-study result.

Value

An object of class mfrm_generalizability with:

variance_components

One row per random effect plus residual, with columns Source, Variance, ProportionVariance, and Identified. When Identified is false, the fitted allocation and its proportion are not uniquely determined by the source design.

coefficients

One-row data frame with G (generalizability coefficient, relative decision) and Phi (dependability coefficient, absolute decision), coefficient status labels, and the identification status of the fitted random-effects model. GReason and PhiReason explain missing coefficients; an empty reason means the point is calculable. ComponentIdentificationChecked records the design check.

design

Description of the crossed-random model. component_identification retains the covariance-kernel Gram matrix, rank, scaled eigenvalues, null space and numerical tolerance. fit_status retains the separate lme4 boundary/convergence assessment.

data_usage

Input source, omission policy, named counts (InputRows, UsedRows, ExcludedRows), excluded_rows, and missing_cells (InputRow, Column). Row positions refer to the supplied data, or stored fitted rows when data = NULL. They cannot recover rows previously removed during MFRM fitting. Counts also accompany the coefficient table and D-study projections, including tabular exports; GStudyDataSource identifies the scope of those counts.

An object of class mfrm_d_study, a data.frame with one row per design scenario and columns for planned facet counts, variance terms, projected G, projected Phi, interpretation bands, and identification status inherited from mfrm_generalizability(). InputRows, UsedRows, and ExcludedRows describe the source G-study, not the planned D-study sample; GStudyDataSource identifies their scope. The data_usage attribute retains its row accounting, including after subsetting. Older source results without accounting have NA counts; they are not assumed to have used all rows. summary(d) returns the coefficient data frame with these saved attributes, rather than generic per-column descriptive statistics. No intervals or new variance-component estimates are computed. GReason, PhiReason, ObjectVarianceReason, RelativeErrorReason, AbsoluteErrorReason and ResidualDivisorReason explain unavailable quantities; empty strings mean no calculation failure. Reasons distinguish unidentified targets, missing/invalid components, zero total variance and numerical range. Fit cautions remain separate in IdentificationStatus and IdentificationNote. ComponentIdentificationChecked and the component_identification attribute retain the source design check.

Invisibly, a ggplot object. plot_data() extracts the scenario table, metric series, axis/group/panel settings, and labels.

Details

The decomposition is on the observed numeric Score scale. It does not use the fitted MFRM latent scale or estimate a latent ordinal G/Phi coefficient.

Fits the main-effects Gaussian linear mixed model Score ~ 1 + (1 | Person) + (1 | Facet1) + ... + Residual (G = sigma2(p) / (sigma2(p) + sigma2(Residual)); Phi adds facet main-effect variances before D-study scaling). Person-by-facet and facet-by-facet interactions are omitted and absorbed into Residual (use mfrm_g_study() when interaction components are required).

Component identification and boundaries: Linear independence of observation covariance kernels (after REML intercept projection) determines Identified in variance_components and design$component_identification separately from lme4::isSingular() (design$fit_status). Identified sums can still supply Phi when individual confounded allocations cannot support unequal future D-study counts (GStatus, PhiStatus, IdentificationStatus; zero total variance gives zero_total_variance).

The projection uses the variance decomposition already estimated by mfrm_generalizability(). For a random measurement facet j, main-effect variance contributes sigma2_j / n_j to the absolute-error denominator. Under the fitted additive model, residual errors are independent across observations. For a complete future crossing with common facet levels for all persons, their mean has variance sigma2_Residual / prod(n_j). Facet-wide shifts cancel from relative comparisons but enter absolute error as sum(sigma2_j / n_j). This justifies "highest_order" within that model. If omitted interactions actually exist, the fitted residual does not recover their separate variances or correlations; dividing it by the product is then an assumption. "single_condition" and "none" are alternative planning assumptions, not estimates of these correlations, confidence bounds, or a guarantee that the true projection lies between them. The relative-decision denominator uses only this scaled residual term. Missing or invalid required components leave the affected coefficient unavailable; they are not zero variance. These are point projections conditional on estimated components, not uncertainty bounds or automatic recommendations for sample size. Returned G/Phi retain full precision, as do the values used for their reference-status labels. Round only for presentation, after any comparisons.

Error variances are evaluated independently of object variance: they remain available when object variance is zero or missing. Zero object variance with positive error gives a coefficient of zero; zero total variance is undefined. For checked sources, only identified variance sums enter the output. For example, two confounded facet main effects can still contribute their identified sum when their planned counts are equal; unequal counts require the separate, unidentified components. Coefficients use scaled sums to avoid overflow. A coefficient can therefore remain calculable even when its error variance exceeds floating-point range. Such unrepresentable quantities are returned as NA with reasons.

This is a pragmatic D-study planning layer, not a full p x r x i ANOVA decomposition. If person-by-rater or person-by-item interactions are a primary estimand, consider mfrm_g_study() and mfrm_d_study() for one or two common random facets, including Person-by-Task, Person-by-Rater, and Person-by-Rater-by-Task. Those functions also accept a single score and estimate the corresponding interaction components explicitly. Changing residual_scaling here only explores assumptions; it does not estimate the omitted interactions.

Pass the result directly to mfrm_report() for full projection tables and their assumptions. Newly created results retain source variance components, estimation settings and observed facet counts. Reports of older compatible results mark missing source details not_recorded; report creation never reconstructs components or computes confidence intervals.

The G and Phi values returned here belong to the generalizability-theory metric family. They should not be interpreted as coefficient alpha, omega, KR-20, or IRT marginal/separation reliability, even though all of those summaries may be displayed on a 0–1 scale in broader reporting dashboards. They remain on the observed numeric score scale inherited from mfrm_generalizability(), not the fitted MFRM latent scale.

Points represent requested scenarios; connecting lines and contours are visual guides. Missing estimates remain missing and break curves. If none are available, inspect the D-study table and source variance components. No reference lines are drawn by default. Specify reference = c(0.70, 0.80) to reproduce the earlier coefficient guides. User-chosen guides are not universal acceptance criteria or confidence bounds; their values and interpretation remain in the returned plot data. Heatmaps include a numeric color key; exact values remain in the table.

The main-effects G-study combines unmodeled interactions in its residual. Different residual-scaling curves describe assumptions, not confidence bounds. All projections hold estimated components fixed. Check source fit warnings before interpreting even large coefficients. For supported designs with separately estimated interactions, including a single score, use mfrm_g_study() and mfrm_d_study().

Session plot defaults

See mfrmr_visual_diagnostics for options(mfrmr.plot_preset), argument precedence, and appearance when saving or reusing a plot.

References

Bates, D., Maechler, M., Bolker, B., & Walker, S. (2015). Fitting linear mixed-effects models using lme4. Journal of Statistical Software, 67(1), 1–48. doi:10.18637/jss.v067.i01 . Gaussian ML/REML model and optimization. See also lme4::isSingular() for the meaning of a singular fitted covariance matrix.

Cronbach, L. J., Gleser, G. C., Nanda, H., & Rajaratnam, N. (1972). The dependability of behavioral measurements: Theory of generalizability for scores and profiles. Wiley.

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability theory. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0 . General G/D framework; the main-effects restriction and residual-scaling choices here are package-specific limits.

Cronbach, L. J., Gleser, G. C., Nanda, H., & Rajaratnam, N. (1972). The dependability of behavioral measurements: Theory of generalizability for scores and profiles. Wiley.

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability theory. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0 . This framework does not recover the interaction components omitted by the source main-effects model.

Examples

# Saved synthetic JML/RSM analysis of example_core.
# For your own data, fit a model first; see ?fit_mfrm.
example_fit <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "core-jml.rds", package = "mfrmr"))
fit <- example_fit$fit
if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {
  gt <- mfrm_generalizability(fit)
  gt$variance_components
  # Look for: a Person variance component well above any single
  #   non-person facet's variance share. Large rater or criterion
  #   variance shares mean those conditions add measurement error
  #   relative to person spread.
  gt$coefficients
  # Compare G and Phi with study-specific requirements; 0.70 and 0.80
  #   are reference guides only. Phi < G means absolute decisions are noisier than relative
  #   decisions; review whether facet main effects need anchoring.
  # Always check IdentificationStatus before using the bands:
  gt$coefficients[, c("G", "Phi", "GStatus", "PhiStatus",
                      "IdentificationStatus")]
  gt$design$identification_note
  # If IdentificationStatus is not "identified", treat G/Phi as
  # design-review evidence rather than decision-ready reliability.
}
#> [1] "No lme4 boundary or singular fit was detected."
# Saved synthetic JML/RSM analysis of example_core.
# For your own data, fit a model first; see ?fit_mfrm.
example_fit <- readRDS(system.file("examples", "core-jml.rds", package = "mfrmr"))
fit <- example_fit$fit
if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {
  gt <- mfrm_generalizability(fit)
  ds <- mfrm_d_study(gt, data.frame(Rater = c(2, 3, 4), Criterion = 4))
  ds[, c("n_Rater", "n_Criterion", "G", "Phi",
         "GStatus", "PhiStatus", "IdentificationStatus")]
  # If IdentificationStatus is not "identified", even large G/Phi
  # values remain identification warnings, not decision-ready evidence.
}
#> mfrmr D-study projection
#>   Object of measurement: Person 
#>   Random facets: Rater, Criterion 
#> 
#>   Estimand scale: observed numeric score
#>   G-study rows: 768 input; 768 used; 0 excluded.
#>   Counts start from stored fitted rows; earlier MFRM filtering is not included.
#>   Residual assumption: Divide residual by all facet counts 
#> 
#>  n_Rater n_Criterion         G       Phi
#>        2           4 0.8240540 0.7887498
#>        3           4 0.8753947 0.8447234
#>        4           4 0.9035412 0.8757990
#>   Observed-score planning projections hold estimated variance components fixed.
#>   They do not establish cut-score accuracy or an adequate rating design.
#> 
#>   Note: 0.70 and 0.80 are reference guides, not universal decision rules.
# After creating ds with mfrm_d_study():
# plot(ds, x_var = "n_Rater", panel_grid = c("Metric", "ResidualScaling"))
# For Rater x Task x Occasion scenarios, separate occasions explicitly:
# plot(ds, type = "heatmap", x_var = "n_Rater", y_var = "n_Task",
#      metric = "Phi", panel_by = "n_Occasion")
# With residual_scaling = "sensitivity", use
# panel_grid = c("n_Occasion", "ResidualScaling") instead.
